abstract: This article argues for a methodological return to URL (link) analysis as a tool for cross-platform controversy mapping, challenging the assumption that link studies became obsolete with the rise of platformization. Using the decade-long debate over the construction of a shipping canal through the Vistula Spit in Poland, the author analyzes 21,756 Facebook posts and 133,814 tweets to show that URLs still function as reliable controversy indicators, but in platform-specific ways. The study connects early digital methods with contemporary platformization research and CSCW work on socio-technical systems, treating links as traceable artifacts through which platform affordances become visible.
key_claims: URLs remain valuable analytical objects for studying cross-platform controversies despite being largely abandoned after platformization shifted research toward hashtags, keywords, and platform-native metrics.

Links are not neutral carriers of information but socio-technical artifacts (non-human actors/mediators in Actor-Network Theory terms) whose meaning and function depend on the design and affordances of the platform in which they are used.
On Twitter, links foreground political sentiment, alignment, and polarization, while on Facebook they foreground protest mobilization and local/community organization.
These platform differences can be explained by platform affordances, which structure not only the circulation of content but also its meaning within controversies.

Link-based traces allow controversies to be studied across platforms without relying exclusively on discursive or semantic analysis, bridging early digital methods with CSCW research on socio-technical systems and platform affordances.
methods: Mixed-methods controversy mapping focused on a single digital object: URLs published in posts about the Vistula Spit Canal controversy on Facebook and Twitter.

Data collection across 2016–2023: Twitter data retrieved via university Twitter API access through the 4CAT tool; Facebook data retrieved via CrowdTangle, using identical phrase-search keywords on both platforms.

A nested two-query design: a 'core collection' using bare object-phrase names of the controversy and an 'extended collection' pairing those phrases with discourse terms, slogans, and hashtags from both supporters and opponents.
Dataset of 21,756 Facebook posts and 133,814 tweets; quantitative analysis of frequency and distribution of digital objects (likes, shares, retweets, mentions, hashtags, URLs).

Network analysis in Gephi connecting accounts that shared the same URLs, spatialized with the ForceAtlas2 layout and clustered using modularity-based community detection (Blondel et al. 2008), followed by manual coding into seven link categories (news, local news, economic news, conservative sites, far-right sites, suspicious websites, informational sites) using external ratings such as Media Bias/Fact Check.
findings: Linking was a prominent practice on both platforms but played different roles: on Twitter external linking was common (48.7% core, 61.8% extended) and highly self-referential (up to ~52% of links in the extended collection pointed back to Twitter), traveling with retweets and mentions in an economy of amplification.

On Facebook over 90% of posts contained links (93% core, 94% extended) irrespective of collection, a near-universal default even though Facebook's 2018 feed change deprioritized external-publisher content; link posts drew more comments than link-free posts, consistent with the controversy generating the interaction the ranking favored.

Twitter link clusters in the extended collection were dense and polarized, concentrating around conservative, far-right, and suspicious (including Russian-affiliated) sites set against a news cluster, bridged mainly by self-referential platform-internal links—suggesting links serve as markers of alignment rather than evidence.

Facebook link clusters were more dispersed and oriented outward, linking to local news, environmental and pro-environmental groups, grassroots protest accounts, and far-right sites, with links functioning evidentially and as mobilizing resources for collective action.

The same mainstream news resources were mobilized by different political camps across platforms (e.g., state broadcaster TVP circulated within Twitter's conservative/nationalist segment, while mainstream portals were shared by center-left accounts on Facebook).
contributions: Demonstrates that URLs can serve as platform-specific indicators of how participants engage with a controversy (polarization on Twitter versus mobilization on Facebook).
Shows these differences are explained by platform affordances, which shape the meaning and function of links, not just their circulation.

Argues for a methodological return to link analysis as a tool for cross-platform controversy mapping, bringing digital methods into dialogue with CSCW research on socio-technical systems and online collaboration.

Reframes links as active mediators rather than residual artifacts, and offers link-tracing as a practical, trace-based method for detecting contested issues, influential sources, and the spread of potentially misleading content across platforms.
framing: The paper situates itself at the intersection of controversy mapping (an empirical application of Actor-Network Theory), internet/web studies of platformization and link economies (Helmond, Gerlitz, Rogers), and CSCW research on socio-technical systems and platform affordances. It positions links as non-human actors and traceable artifacts, arguing against treating platforms as neutral channels and reviving early digital-methods link analysis for the contemporary platformized web.
